title: JavaScript Web Stack Cheat Sheet

introduction.heading: JavaScript, TypeScript, Node.js, Express, React, Next.js and Tailwind at a Glance
introduction.description: These seven names come up together constantly, but they are not alternatives to each other: some are languages, some run in the browser, some run on a server, and one only does styling. This sheet compares them side by side, then gives each one a one-sentence description of what it is for and a small example. All the examples are variations on the same idea - a user named Ada - so you can see how the pieces differ without learning a new problem each time.

prerequisites: Basic familiarity with HTML and how a web page is loaded in a browser
Node.js installed if you want to run the JavaScript, Node.js and Express examples (`node --version` to check)

steps.title: The Seven at a Glance
steps.description: One row per technology: what kind of thing it is, what it builds on, where it runs, and what you reach for it to do.

rows: Logic and interactivity - the base everything else here is made from
Catching type mistakes before the code runs
Running JavaScript outside the browser: scripts, servers, build tools
REST APIs and web servers with routes and middleware
Building interactive interfaces out of reusable components
Whole sites: file-based routing, server rendering, API routes
Styling with small utility classes written right in the markup

steps.note: Only JavaScript and TypeScript are languages. Node.js is where JavaScript runs on a server, React and Tailwind are for what the user sees, and Express and Next.js are frameworks built on top of the others.

steps.title: How They Fit Together
steps.description: Sort them by the layer of the app they belong to. A typical project takes one choice per layer.

rows: TypeScript for anything that will grow; plain JavaScript for small scripts and learning
React builds the structure and behavior, Tailwind the look - they do not overlap
Node.js runs the code, Express organizes the routes - you always need the first to use the second
Replaces a separate React app and Express server when one project should do both

steps.note: A common setup is a React front end (styled with Tailwind) talking to an Express API, all in TypeScript. Next.js is the alternative that puts the front end and the back end in one project.

steps.title: JavaScript
steps.description: The language of the web: it makes pages interactive in the browser and, with Node.js, also runs on servers.
steps.note: **Compare:** JavaScript has no type checking - `age: "36"` is accepted silently and fails later, at run time. That gap is exactly what TypeScript fills.

steps.title: TypeScript
steps.description: JavaScript plus types: you describe the shape of your data, and the compiler flags mistakes before you run anything.
steps.note: **Compare:** TypeScript is not a different language to learn from scratch - every valid JavaScript file is valid TypeScript. Browsers and Node.js do not run it directly, so it is compiled to plain JavaScript first.

steps.title: Node.js
steps.description: A runtime that executes JavaScript outside the browser, so you can read files, run scripts and start servers.
steps.note: **Compare:** Node.js is not a framework - it is where the code runs. Its built-in `http` module can serve requests on its own, but routing and parsing quickly get repetitive, which is why Express exists. The imports above need `"type": "module"` in `package.json`.

steps.title: Express.js
steps.description: A small framework on top of Node.js that turns incoming requests into routes, so you can build an API in a few lines.
steps.note: **Compare:** Express gives you the server and the API but no pages and no UI - you pair it with a front end such as React. Next.js can replace both with a single project.

steps.title: React
steps.description: A library for building user interfaces from components - functions that return markup and re-render when their state changes.
steps.note: **Compare:** React only draws the UI. It has no router, no server and no data fetching built in, which is why larger apps add a framework such as Next.js around it.

steps.title: Next.js
steps.description: A framework around React that adds routing, server rendering and API endpoints, so a page can fetch its data on the server before it reaches the browser.
steps.note: **Compare:** In plain React you would wire up a router and fetch the user in an effect after the page loads. In Next.js the folder name `[id]` becomes the route, and the data is already in the HTML when the page arrives.

steps.title: Tailwind CSS
steps.description: A CSS framework made of small single-purpose classes, so you style an element by listing classes on it instead of writing a separate stylesheet.
steps.note: **Compare:** Tailwind only handles looks and works with any of the above. In React and Next.js the attribute is written `className` instead of `class`. It does not replace CSS knowledge - the class names are CSS properties in shorthand.

gettingStarted.heading: Which One Do I Need?
steps: Make a page interactive, or learn programming - **JavaScript**
Same, but with fewer bugs in a growing codebase - **TypeScript**
Run JavaScript on your computer or a server - **Node.js**
Build a whole site with routing and server rendering in one project - **Next.js**
Style it without writing separate CSS files - **Tailwind CSS**
